sections.title: Babylon as a Place of Exile

blocks.text: Babylon was not merely a symbol in this chapter but a major political, religious, economic, and scribal center where displaced Judeans had to build ordinary lives. Jeremiah therefore speaks about houses, gardens, families, and the city's welfare within a real imperial setting. The surviving kinds of Babylonian records reflect different institutions and social levels, so no single kind gives a complete picture of the city or empire. Judean communities also continued in Babylonia after return movements began, showing that return did not mean every deportee or descendant left.

The commands to build, plant, marry, multiply, and seek Babylon's peace address the deported community collectively. Together they present exile as a long-term condition and challenge prophets promising a quick return. The promise associated with seventy years places restoration beyond the immediate hopes being promoted in Babylon. How that period should be understood became a matter of later interpretation in Chronicles, Daniel, and other Second Temple writings.

The book of Jeremiah contains poetry, prose sermons, narratives, letters, headings, repeated accounts, restoration collections, oracles concerning nations, and an appendix. Jeremiah 29's correspondence is therefore one form within a varied book. A practical outline of the Masoretic form groups chapters 26–29 together, followed by the restoration collection in chapters 30–33, though this outline does not settle questions about the book's long compositional and textual history.
